unit.name: Theme B: Religion & Life
unit.subtitle: Origins of the universe, value of life, animal rights, and environmental responsibility

lessons.title: Origins of the Universe & Human Life
lessons.description: Religious and scientific views on how the universe and human life began.
lessons.content_html:
Religious Teachings on the Origin of the Universe

One of the biggest questions humans ask is: how did the universe begin? Religious traditions offer explanations through their sacred texts, while science proposes theories based on evidence. The specification requires you to understand both perspectives and how they relate to each other.

Christianity: The Bible describes God creating the universe in six days and resting on the seventh (Genesis 1). God created light, sky, land, plants, animals and finally humans. Genesis 1:1 states: “In the beginning God created the heavens and the earth.” Christians believe God created the universe ex nihilo — out of nothing.

Islam: The Qur’an teaches that Allah created the heavens and the earth in six periods (yawm). Surah 21:30 says “the heavens and the earth used to be joined together and that We ripped them apart.” Allah is the sole creator of everything. The Qur’an (51:47) also states: “We built the universe with great might, and We are certainly expanding it.”

Key Fact

There are different interpretations of these creation accounts. Literalists (or creationists) believe the Bible/Qur’an describes exactly what happened — God created everything in six literal days. Non-literalists believe the creation stories are metaphorical — the “days” represent long periods of time, and the stories teach that God created, not exactly how.

The Big Bang Theory & Religious Views

The Big Bang theory is the leading scientific explanation for the origin of the universe. It proposes that the universe began around 13.8 billion years ago from an extremely hot, dense point that rapidly expanded.

Many religious believers see no conflict between the Big Bang and their faith. They argue that God caused the Big Bang. Non-literal Christians point out that the sequence in Genesis (light, sky, land, plants, animals, humans) broadly matches the scientific order of events. The Qur’an’s reference to the heavens and earth being “joined together, then split apart” (21:30) has been interpreted by some Muslims as describing the Big Bang. Science explains how the universe began; religion explains why.

Creationists reject the Big Bang because it contradicts a literal reading of Genesis. They argue that the universe was created in six 24-hour days as the Bible states. Some point out that the Big Bang cannot explain what existed before the explosion or what caused it — suggesting there must be a creator. Young Earth Creationists believe the universe is around 6,000–10,000 years old, based on biblical genealogies.

Origins of Human Life

Christianity: Genesis 2:7 says God “formed a man from the dust of the ground and breathed into his nostrils the breath of life.” God then created Eve from Adam’s rib. Christians believe humans are unique because they are made in the “image of God” (imago Dei — Genesis 1:27).

Islam: The Qur’an teaches that Allah created Adam from clay (Surah 15:26): “We created man from sounding clay.” Humans are Allah’s finest creation, appointed as khalifah (stewards or caretakers) of the earth.

Evolution & Religious Views

Charles Darwin’s theory of evolution by natural selection proposes that life developed gradually over billions of years from simple organisms. Humans share a common ancestor with other primates.

Many Christians accept evolution as the process God used to create life. Pope Francis stated in 2014: “Evolution in nature is not inconsistent with the notion of creation.” They see evolution as God’s method. However, creationists reject evolution because it contradicts the literal Genesis account.

Many Muslims also accept that evolution may explain how species develop, but most believe that Allah directly created Adam as the first human. Human evolution from apes is generally rejected because the Qur’an describes Adam’s special creation from clay.

The Value of the World

Key Fact

Religious believers see the natural world as valuable because God created it. Two key concepts are dominion (authority over creation — Genesis 1:28: “Rule over the fish in the sea and the birds in the sky”) and stewardship (caring for creation responsibly). Most modern Christians emphasise stewardship over dominion.

In Islam, humans are khalifah — caretakers appointed by Allah to look after the earth. The concept of awe and wonder describes the feeling of amazement at the beauty and complexity of the natural world, which many believers see as evidence of God’s creative power. Psalm 19:1 says: “The heavens declare the glory of God.”

Both Christianity and Islam teach that humans have a responsibility to protect the environment. Christians believe they will be held accountable by God for how they have treated creation. Pope Francis’s encyclical Laudato Si’ (2015) called on all people to protect “our common home.” In Islam, wasting natural resources is considered wrong. The Prophet Muhammad said: “Do not waste water even if you are at a running stream.” On the Day of Judgement, Muslims believe they will answer to Allah for how they treated the earth.
lessons.exam_tip_html: For questions on creation and science, avoid saying religion and science always disagree. Many believers accept both. The best answers show how religious believers reconcile science with their faith — for example, by interpreting Genesis metaphorically or seeing God as the cause behind the Big Bang. Use the phrase “non-literal interpretation” to show the examiner you understand this nuance.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Christianity and Islam both teach that God/Allah created the universe. Literalists believe in six-day creation; non-literalists see the accounts as metaphorical and compatible with the Big Bang.
  • Evolution is accepted by many religious believers as God’s method, but creationists reject it. Islam generally accepts biological evolution but not that humans evolved from other species.
  • Stewardship (caring for creation) and dominion (authority over it) are key concepts. Both religions teach that humans have a responsibility to protect the natural world.

practice_questions.text: 'Science has made religious teachings about the origin of the universe irrelevant.' Evaluate this statement. In your answer you should give reasoned arguments in support of this statement, give reasoned arguments to support a different point of view, refer to religious arguments, and reach a justified conclusion.
practice_questions.marks:
Arguments in support:
• The Big Bang theory is supported by scientific evidence (cosmic microwave background radiation, expansion of the universe) while religious accounts have no empirical evidence.
• Evolution explains human origins without needing a creator.
• A literal six-day creation contradicts scientific dating of the universe at 13.8 billion years.
• Humanists argue that science provides testable, reliable explanations while religious accounts are matters of faith.
Arguments against:
• Science cannot explain what caused the Big Bang or why the universe exists — religion answers these deeper questions.
• Many scientists are religious — Pope Francis accepted evolution, showing science and faith can coexist.
• Non-literal interpretations of Genesis are compatible with the Big Bang.
• Religious teachings give life meaning and purpose, which science alone cannot provide.
• The Qur’an’s description of the universe being 'split apart' (21:30) could be seen as describing the Big Bang.
Top band (10-12): A well-argued response with two clear sides, specific religious teachings and a justified conclusion.
Upper-mid band (7-9): Good reasoning with some religious knowledge but may lack balance.
Lower-mid band (4-6): Some relevant points but limited development or one-sided.
Lower band (1-3): Simple statements with little reasoning.

lessons.title: The Environment & Animal Rights
lessons.description: Religious teachings on environmental responsibility and the ethical treatment of animals.
lessons.content_html:
Use & Abuse of the Environment

The environment faces serious threats from human activity. Pollution of air, water and land damages ecosystems and harms human health. Climate change, driven by the burning of fossil fuels, threatens the future of the planet. Religious believers see protecting the environment as a moral duty.

The use of natural resources such as oil, gas, coal, water and timber is essential for modern life. However, many of these resources are finite — they will eventually run out. Religious teachings call on humans to use resources responsibly, not wastefully.

Key Fact

Christians believe in stewardship — caring for creation on God’s behalf. Genesis 2:15 says God placed humans in the Garden of Eden “to work it and take care of it.” Pope Francis’s encyclical Laudato Si’ (2015) described the earth as “our common home” and called for urgent action on climate change and pollution.

Muslims believe humans are khalifah (caretakers) of the earth. The Qur’an (6:165) says: “It is He who has made you successors upon the earth.” Wasting resources is considered wrong. The Prophet Muhammad taught: “Do not waste water even if you are at a running stream.” Muslims believe they will be accountable to Allah on the Day of Judgement for how they treated the environment.

Many religious organisations actively campaign for environmental protection. Christian organisations like A Rocha work on conservation projects worldwide. The Church of England has committed to achieving net zero carbon emissions by 2030. Islamic Relief has environmental programmes addressing deforestation and water pollution. The Islamic Declaration on Global Climate Change (2015) urged Muslims to take action based on their role as khalifah. These responses show that religious environmental teaching is not just theoretical — it drives real-world action.

Use & Abuse of Animals

Humans use animals in many ways: for food, clothing, medical research, entertainment and companionship. Religious traditions have varying views on how animals should be treated and whether these uses are morally acceptable.

Key Fact

Both Christianity and Islam teach that animals are part of God’s creation and should be treated with respect. However, most religious traditions accept that humans have a higher status than animals. Genesis 1:28 gives humans dominion (authority) over animals. The Qur’an says Allah “subjected to you whatever is in the heavens and on the earth” (45:13).

Animal Experimentation

Animal experimentation involves testing medicines, treatments or products on animals. This is one of the three “contrasting beliefs” topics in this theme — you must be able to explain different religious views.

In favour: Many Christians accept animal experimentation if it is necessary to save human lives or reduce suffering. Humans have dominion over animals (Genesis 1:28) and are uniquely made in God’s image. The Catholic Church teaches that animal experimentation is morally acceptable “if it remains within reasonable limits and contributes to caring for or saving human lives.”

Against: Some Christians, particularly Quakers, oppose animal experimentation because it causes unnecessary suffering. They argue that stewardship means protecting all of God’s creatures. Proverbs 12:10 says: “The righteous care for the needs of their animals.” The RSPCA was founded by an Anglican clergyman, reflecting Christian concern for animal welfare.

In favour (with conditions): Some Muslim scholars permit animal experimentation if it is genuinely necessary for medical advances and there is no alternative. Saving human life is a high priority in Islam: “Whoever saves a life, it is as if he has saved all of humanity” (Qur’an 5:32).

Against: Islam generally opposes unnecessary harm to animals. The Prophet Muhammad said: “If anyone wrongfully kills even a sparrow, he will have to answer for it on the Day of Judgement.” Animals are part of Allah’s creation and deserve compassion. Causing pain for cosmetic testing or trivial purposes is considered haram (forbidden).

The Use of Animals for Food

Both Christianity and Islam allow eating meat, but both have rules about how animals should be treated. Christians have no specific dietary laws (Jesus declared all foods clean in Mark 7:19), though many Christians choose to eat less meat or become vegetarian out of concern for animal welfare and the environment.

Islam requires that meat be halal (permissible). Animals must be slaughtered humanely in the name of Allah, with a sharp knife to minimise suffering. Pork is haram. The Qur’an (5:3) lists forbidden foods. These rules reflect Islam’s teaching that animals should be treated with respect even when used for food.

Key Fact

Non-religious perspectives on animal rights are also important. The philosopher Peter Singer argues that animals have the capacity to suffer and therefore deserve moral consideration. Vegetarians and vegans often argue that it is wrong to use animals for food when plant-based alternatives exist. Animal rights organisations like the RSPCA campaign against factory farming and animal cruelty.
lessons.exam_tip_html: For the contrasting beliefs question on animal experimentation, make sure you compare a Christian view with an Islamic view (or two different Christian views). Each point needs: (1) what the belief is, (2) why they believe it, and (3) ideally a scripture reference. For example: “Many Christians accept animal experimentation because humans have dominion over animals (Genesis 1:28) and saving human life takes priority.”
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Christians believe in stewardship of the environment (Genesis 2:15, Laudato Si’). Muslims believe humans are khalifah (caretakers) accountable to Allah.
  • Animal experimentation is a contrasting beliefs topic: most Christians accept it within limits (dominion), while Islam generally opposes unnecessary harm but may permit it for life-saving research.
  • Both religions allow eating meat but expect animals to be treated humanely. Islam requires halal slaughter. Some religious and non-religious people choose vegetarianism for ethical reasons.

lessons.title: Abortion & Euthanasia
lessons.description: Sanctity of life, quality of life, and contrasting beliefs on abortion and euthanasia.
lessons.content_html:
Sanctity of Life & Quality of Life

Two key concepts underpin religious and ethical debates about abortion and euthanasia. The sanctity of life is the belief that all human life is sacred because it is created by God. Christians point to Genesis 1:27: “God created mankind in his own image.” Muslims believe Allah breathes a soul into every person: ‘Then He proportioned him and breathed into him of His Spirit’ (Qur’an 32:9).

The quality of life is a different concept — it considers whether a person’s life is worth living based on their level of comfort, independence, happiness and freedom from pain. Some people argue that when quality of life is extremely poor, ending suffering may be the most compassionate response.

Key Fact

The tension between sanctity of life and quality of life is at the heart of both the abortion and euthanasia debates. Those who prioritise sanctity argue that life must never be deliberately ended. Those who emphasise quality of life argue that sometimes ending suffering is the most loving and compassionate thing to do.

Abortion

Abortion is the deliberate termination of a pregnancy. In England, Scotland and Wales, abortion is legal up to 24 weeks under the Abortion Act 1967 (amended 1990), provided two doctors agree that continuing the pregnancy poses a risk to the physical or mental health of the mother or existing children. After 24 weeks, abortion is only permitted if the mother’s life is at risk or the foetus has a severe abnormality.

Catholic Church: Abortion is always wrong because life begins at conception and is sacred. The Catechism states: “Human life must be respected and protected absolutely from the moment of conception.” The only exception is if a medical procedure to save the mother’s life indirectly causes the death of the foetus (the principle of double effect).

Church of England: Abortion is generally opposed but accepted in certain circumstances, such as when the mother’s life is at risk, in cases of severe foetal abnormality, or after rape. The decision should be made with compassion and careful thought.

Liberal Christians: Some argue that the most loving thing may be to allow abortion in difficult circumstances. They apply Jesus’s teaching of compassion and the principle of “the lesser of two evils.”

Most Muslim scholars oppose abortion after ensoulment (when the soul enters the body), traditionally believed to occur at 120 days. Before this point, some scholars permit abortion in certain circumstances, such as when the mother’s life is in danger. The Qur’an (17:31) warns: “Do not kill your children for fear of poverty.”

If the mother’s life is at risk, most scholars agree that her life takes priority because she has existing responsibilities and relationships. However, abortion for convenience or non-medical reasons is generally considered haram.

Euthanasia

Euthanasia means deliberately ending someone’s life to relieve suffering. It is sometimes called “mercy killing.” There are different types: voluntary euthanasia (the person requests it), non-voluntary euthanasia (the person cannot give consent, e.g. in a coma), and assisted suicide (helping someone end their own life). All forms of euthanasia and assisted suicide are illegal in the UK.

Key Fact

Both Christianity and Islam oppose euthanasia. Christians believe life is a gift from God and only God should decide when it ends. Job 1:21 says: “The Lord gave and the Lord has taken away.” Islam teaches that only Allah determines the time of death: “No soul can die except by Allah’s leave” (Qur’an 3:145). However, both religions support palliative care to relieve suffering without hastening death.

Arguments for: People should have the right to choose how and when they die. Forcing someone to live in extreme pain is cruel. Quality of life matters — when there is no hope of recovery, euthanasia may be the most compassionate option. Some argue Jesus’s Golden Rule (“Do to others what you would have them do to you” — Matthew 7:12) supports ending suffering.

Arguments against: Life is sacred and belongs to God — humans do not have the right to end it. Euthanasia could lead to a “slippery slope” where vulnerable people feel pressured to die. Modern palliative care can manage pain effectively. The Qur’an teaches patience in suffering: “Allah does not burden a soul beyond that it can bear” (2:286).

Death & the Afterlife

Religious beliefs about what happens after death influence attitudes towards euthanasia and the value of life.

Christianity: Most Christians believe in an afterlife. The soul continues after death — the righteous go to heaven (eternal life with God) and the unrighteous face judgement. Jesus said: “I am the resurrection and the life. The one who believes in me will live, even though they die” (John 11:25). This belief gives Christians hope and comfort in the face of death.

Islam: Muslims believe in Yawm al-Din (the Day of Judgement), when Allah will resurrect all people and judge their deeds. The righteous will enter Jannah (paradise) and the wicked will be sent to Jahannam (hell). This belief means Muslims see life as a test and believe suffering has a purpose — it builds patience and strengthens faith.

Belief in an afterlife reinforces opposition to euthanasia. If this life is a preparation for eternal life, then cutting it short may have spiritual consequences. Christians may fear that taking one’s own life or assisting death goes against God’s plan. Muslims believe that accepting suffering patiently is rewarded in the afterlife. However, some non-religious people argue that without an afterlife, reducing suffering in this life becomes even more important — supporting the case for euthanasia.

Key Fact

Humanists and atheists, who do not believe in an afterlife, argue that moral decisions should focus on reducing suffering in this life. They may support euthanasia because they believe people have the right to die with dignity. This contrasts with religious views that see suffering as meaningful and life as belonging to God.
lessons.exam_tip_html: For the 12-mark evaluate question on abortion or euthanasia, you must include religious arguments on both sides and a clear conclusion. A common mistake is only giving one religion’s view. Use specific teachings: “The Lord gave and the Lord has taken away” (Job 1:21) for euthanasia, or the Catholic Catechism on abortion. Include a non-religious perspective (e.g. humanist) for extra depth. Always weigh up the arguments before reaching your own reasoned conclusion.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • The sanctity of life (all life is sacred) and quality of life (suffering matters) are the two key principles in abortion and euthanasia debates.
  • Both Christianity and Islam generally oppose abortion, but there is a range of views. Catholics oppose it absolutely; the Church of England and many Muslims accept it in certain circumstances, especially when the mother’s life is at risk.
  • Euthanasia is illegal in the UK and opposed by both religions. Christians and Muslims believe only God should decide when life ends, and both support palliative care as an alternative.

lessons.title: Abortion and Euthanasia
lessons.description: When does life begin? The right to die? Religious and ethical views on both issues.
lessons.content_html:
Abortion

Abortion is the deliberate termination of a pregnancy. It remains one of the most debated moral issues in modern society. Before 1967, abortion was illegal in the UK, and women resorted to dangerous “back street” abortions that led to infections, injuries, and deaths.

Key Fact

Under the Abortion Act 1967, amended in 1990, abortion is legal in England, Scotland and Wales up to 24 weeks if two doctors agree that at least one condition applies: the mother’s life is at risk, there is risk to her physical or mental health, there is a significant chance the baby would be born with severe disabilities, or an additional child would affect the wellbeing of existing children.

Christian Views on Abortion

Christians hold a range of views on abortion, but all agree that human life has special value because it is created by God.

The Roman Catholic Church teaches that abortion is always wrong. Catholics believe life begins at conception and that destroying a foetus is equivalent to murder. This is rooted in the sanctity of life — the idea that life is sacred because God created it. The Bible states: “You shall not murder” (Exodus 20:13). Catholics apply this directly to abortion.

The Bible also suggests God has a plan for every life before birth: “Before I formed you in the womb I knew you, before you were born I set you apart” (Jeremiah 1:5). Psalm 139:13 adds: “For you created my inmost being; you knit me together in my mother’s womb.”

However, other Christians, including many Anglicans and Methodists, believe abortion may be acceptable in certain circumstances. Jesus taught that the most important thing is love (agape), and it may be the most loving action to allow abortion if the mother’s life is at risk or the pregnancy resulted from rape. As Colossians 3:12 says: “Clothe yourselves with compassion, kindness, humility, gentleness and patience.”

Pro-life supporters believe the foetus has a right to life from conception and that abortion is morally wrong. They argue adoption is always an alternative. Pro-choice supporters believe a woman should have the right to decide what happens to her own body. They argue that a foetus is not yet a person, especially in early pregnancy, and that forcing a woman to continue an unwanted pregnancy can cause serious harm.

Islamic Views on Abortion

Muslims believe human life is precious because it is given by Allah. The Qur’an teaches: “Do not kill your children for fear of poverty — We shall provide for them and for you — killing them is a great sin” (Qur’an 17:31). This verse is widely used to argue that abortion for financial reasons is haram (forbidden).

A key concept in Islam is ensoulment — the moment when the foetus receives its soul from Allah. Many scholars place this at 120 days after conception. Before ensoulment, some Muslims believe abortion may be permitted if the mother’s life is in danger. After ensoulment, abortion is generally forbidden because the foetus is considered a living being with a soul.

The Qur’an also warns: “If anyone kills a person — unless in retribution for murder or spreading corruption in the land — it is as if he kills all mankind” (Qur’an 5:32) — a Qur’anic verse that records a ruling originally given to the Children of Israel, though Islamic scholars widely apply this life-sanctity principle universally. Most Muslims agree that the mother’s life takes priority over the life of the foetus.

Euthanasia

Euthanasia comes from the Greek words eu (good) and thanatos (death), meaning “a good death.” All forms of euthanasia are currently illegal in the UK and treated as murder or manslaughter.

Key Fact

Active euthanasia is taking deliberate action to end a life, such as giving a lethal injection. Passive euthanasia is allowing someone to die by withdrawing or withholding treatment. Voluntary euthanasia is when the patient requests death. Non-voluntary euthanasia is when the patient cannot give consent, for example because they are in a coma.

Tony Bland was 18 when he attended the Hillsborough football stadium in 1989. A crush killed 94 people on the day and left Tony in a persistent vegetative state (PVS) with irreversible brain damage. Although there was no hope of recovery, he was kept alive through tubes providing food and fluids. In 1993, the hospital and his parents obtained court permission to withdraw treatment. Tony became the first patient in UK legal history to be allowed to die through the withdrawal of life-prolonging treatment. The law did not classify this as passive euthanasia.

In September 2015, the British Parliament rejected plans for a “right to die” law in England and Wales. 118 MPs voted in favour and 330 against allowing terminally ill adults to end their lives with medical supervision. In countries such as Belgium and the Netherlands, euthanasia is legal under strict conditions — the patient must request it, their suffering must be unbearable, and two doctors must be consulted.

Christian Views on Euthanasia

Most Christians oppose euthanasia because of the sanctity of life. The Ten Commandments state “You shall not murder” (Exodus 20:13), and Psalm 139:16 teaches that God has ordained every day of a person’s life. The Salvation Army has stated: “All people deserve compassion and care in suffering and dying. Euthanasia and assisted suicide should not, however, be considered acceptable responses. They undermine human dignity and are morally wrong.”

However, some Christians accept the principle of double effect — where medicine given to relieve pain may shorten life as a side effect. They see this as different from intentional killing because the primary intention is to reduce suffering, not to cause death. Many Christians actively support hospice care and palliative care as compassionate alternatives to euthanasia. Jesus taught “Blessed are the merciful” (Matthew 5:7), and Christians apply this by caring for the dying with dignity.

For: People deserve to die with dignity. If someone’s quality of life is very low, it may be more compassionate to let them die. Everyone should have the right to decide how they die. Against: Someone might recover. It is a “slippery slope” that could lead to abuse. No one should carry the burden of deciding another person’s death. It devalues the sanctity of life. As Dr Gunning warned: “Once you accept killing as a solution to a single problem, you will find tomorrow hundreds of problems for which killing can be seen as a solution.”

Islamic Views on Euthanasia

Islam is firmly opposed to all forms of euthanasia. Muslims believe in predestination — that Allah has planned every person’s life, and to end life prematurely is to interfere with His plan. The Qur’an states: “No soul may die except with God’s permission at a predestined time” (Qur’an 3:145), and “Do not kill each other, for God is merciful to you” (Qur’an 4:29).

Key Fact

Euthanasia is haram in Islam. Muslims believe all life is a gift from Allah and only Allah decides when it ends. Suffering may be a test of faith, and caring for the sick is an opportunity to do good that helps a person gain entry to paradise. Unlike some Christians, most Muslim scholars reject even the principle of double effect.
lessons.exam_tip_html: When answering questions on abortion and euthanasia, always include both Christian and Islamic perspectives with specific teachings or quotes. For 12-mark evaluation questions, present arguments for and against the statement, include religious and non-religious views, use key terms like “sanctity of life” and “quality of life,” and finish with a clear personal conclusion. Remember to explain why believers hold their views — not just state what they believe.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Abortion is legal in the UK up to 24 weeks under specific conditions. Christians hold diverse views, from the Catholic total ban to more liberal positions. Islam permits abortion before ensoulment (120 days) in limited circumstances, especially if the mother’s life is at risk.
  • All forms of euthanasia are illegal in the UK. Both Christianity and Islam oppose euthanasia based on the sanctity of life, though some Christians accept the principle of double effect. Islam considers euthanasia haram because only Allah determines when life ends.
  • The tension between sanctity of life and quality of life is central to both debates — religious believers must balance respect for God-given life with compassion for those who are suffering.

lessons.title: Death and an Afterlife
lessons.description: Christian and Muslim beliefs about what happens after death and how they shape the value of life.
lessons.content_html:
What Happens After We Die?

One of the biggest questions humans have ever asked is what happens after death. Different religions and worldviews give very different answers. For this theme, you need to understand akhirah (the Islamic concept of life after death), Christian beliefs about the afterlife, and how non-religious people respond to the question.

These beliefs are not just abstract ideas — they directly shape how people value human life and make moral decisions while they are alive.

Key Fact

Christians and Muslims believe in heaven (paradise) and hell. Some Christians, such as Catholics, also believe in purgatory. Non-religious people generally do not believe in any afterlife.

Christian Beliefs About the Afterlife

Christians believe that after death, people face judgement from God. Those who have lived according to God’s will are rewarded with eternal life in heaven, while those who have rejected God face eternal separation from him in hell.

There are two main Christian beliefs about how the afterlife works:

Immortality of the soul — Some Christians believe the soul is eternal and continues living immediately after death. Jesus told the thief on the cross: “Truly I tell you, today you will be with me in Paradise” (Luke 23:43). This suggests the afterlife begins straight away.

Resurrection of the body — Other Christians believe that the dead will be physically raised at the end of time. Bible verses describe people “rising from their graves,” suggesting a future bodily resurrection on Judgement Day.

Some Christians, including Catholics, believe in both — the soul lives on after death but will be reunited with a resurrected body at the end of time.

Purgatory is a state that some Christians, particularly Catholics, believe people go to after death in order to atone for their sins before they can enter heaven. It is not a permanent destination but a place of purification.

Many Protestant Christians do not believe in purgatory because Jesus does not mention it directly in the Bible. They believe people go straight to heaven or hell after judgement.

Muslim Beliefs About the Afterlife

In Islam, belief in akhirah (life after death) is one of the six articles of faith. Muslims believe that life on earth is a test from Allah. How a person lives determines what happens to them after death.

Key Fact

Muslims believe that after death, the soul enters a state called barzakh — a waiting period between death and the Day of Judgement. During barzakh, the soul remains in the grave and is questioned by angels about its faith and actions.

On the Day of Judgement, all people will be resurrected and brought before Allah. Their deeds will be weighed, and those who have lived righteously will enter Jannah (paradise), while those who have done evil will be sent to Jahannam (hell).

The Qur’an describes Jannah as a place of gardens, rivers, and eternal peace. Jahannam is described as a place of fire and torment. Muslims believe that living a good life — following the Five Pillars, showing compassion, and obeying Allah — is the way to earn a place in paradise.

Non-Religious Views

Non-religious people, such as atheists and humanists, generally do not believe in any form of afterlife. They argue that science can only prove the existence of the physical world, and there is no evidence for a soul or a spiritual realm. When the body dies, consciousness ends.

Some non-religious people find comfort in the idea that a person’s legacy — their impact on others and the world — continues after they die, even without a supernatural afterlife.

Key Fact

Other religions have different views: Hindus and Sikhs believe in reincarnation — being reborn in a new body after death. Buddhists teach rebirth, but with no permanent soul that passes on. Judaism does not have a single fixed concept of the afterlife.

How Beliefs About Death Affect the Value of Life

Beliefs about what happens after death have a direct impact on how people value human life:

Those who do not believe in an afterlife may value human life more, because they see it as the only life a person has. This can motivate people to make the most of their time and treat others well.

Those who believe in an afterlife may value human life because it is sacred and given by God. However, some may focus more on the afterlife than on earthly life. Christians and Muslims believe that living the way God wants prepares them for life with him after death.

Those who believe in reincarnation may value human life as a means to achieve a better next life through good actions (karma).

For Christians and Muslims, belief in the afterlife reinforces the sanctity of life. Life is valuable because God has given it, and only God should decide when it ends. Muslims believe life is a test — they will be judged on their actions and rewarded or punished accordingly. This belief motivates ethical behaviour and care for others.
lessons.exam_tip_html: When answering questions on death and the afterlife, always compare Christian and Muslim views and use specific religious terminology such as “immortality of the soul,” “resurrection,” “barzakh,” and “Jannah.” For 12-mark evaluation questions, include arguments both for and against the statement, reference scripture, and reach a clear conclusion. Remember to include non-religious perspectives as well as religious ones.
lessons.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Christians believe in heaven and hell; some also believe in purgatory and hold different views on whether the soul is immortal, the body is resurrected, or both.
  • Muslims believe life is a test from Allah, followed by barzakh (waiting), the Day of Judgement, and then Jannah (paradise) or Jahannam (hell).
  • Beliefs about the afterlife directly affect how people value life — whether they see it as sacred, as a test, or as the only existence they will have.

practice_questions.text: Give one Christian belief about what happens after death.
practice_questions.marks:
1 mark for any one valid belief:
• Christians believe in heaven – a state of eternal happiness with God
• Christians believe in hell – eternal separation from God
• Some Christians (e.g. Catholics) believe in purgatory – where souls are purified before entering heaven
• Some Christians believe in the immortality of the soul

practice_questions.text: Explain two different beliefs about life after death. In your answer you should refer to Christianity and Islam.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 2 marks per belief explained (1 mark for a simple point, 2 for a developed point). If beliefs are not contrasting, maximum 2 marks.
• Some Christians believe in the immortality of the soul – that the soul continues living immediately after death, as shown by Jesus telling the thief on the cross he would be in paradise that day (Luke 23:43) (2)
• Muslims believe that after death the soul enters barzakh, a state of waiting, and will not enter Jannah or Jahannam until the Day of Judgement when all people are resurrected and judged by Allah (2)
Alternatively: Christians may believe in purgatory (Catholic view) vs Muslims who do not have a concept of purgatory – in Islam the soul waits in barzakh instead.

practice_questions.text: Explain two religious beliefs about how belief in an afterlife affects the value of human life. Refer to scripture or sacred writings in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Marking: First belief (1–2 marks) + Second belief (1–2 marks) + Source of authority named and applied (1–2 marks) = up to 6 marks.

Award 1 mark per simple point, 2 marks per developed point (maximum 4), plus 1 mark for a relevant reference to scripture or sacred writing.
• Christians believe life is valuable because it is given by God and is sacred. Belief in heaven motivates Christians to live according to God’s will so they can be rewarded with eternal life (2)
• Muslims believe life is a test from Allah. How they live determines whether they enter Jannah or Jahannam, so they are motivated to follow the Five Pillars and treat others with compassion (2)
• Scripture: “Truly I tell you, today you will be with me in Paradise” (Luke 23:43) – shows Christians that the afterlife begins after death, making earthly life a preparation for eternity (1)
OR: “No soul may die except with God’s permission at a predestined time” (Qur’an 3:145) – shows Muslims that God controls life and death (1)

practice_questions.text:
'There must be life after death.' Evaluate this statement. In your answer you should:
• refer to Christian and/or Muslim teachings
• give reasoned arguments to support this statement
• give reasoned arguments to support a different point of view
• reach a justified conclusion.
practice_questions.marks:
Lower band (1-3): One argument with justification.
Lower-mid band (4-6): Different arguments for and against with justification, OR several linked justified arguments for one position.
Upper-mid band (7-9): Good well-justified arguments for and against, linked together.
Top band (10-12): Very well argued. Well-justified arguments for and against, linked together and leading to a reasonable conclusion.
Points for:
• Jesus tells the thief on the cross that he will be in paradise – this implies heaven exists and life continues after death.
• Churches such as the Catholic Church teach that people go to heaven, hell, or purgatory after death.
• Muslims believe in akhirah as one of the six articles of faith – the Qur’an describes Jannah and Jahannam in detail.
• Belief in an afterlife gives life purpose and motivates moral behaviour.
Points against:
• Many Bible verses support resurrection at the end of time rather than immediate afterlife – there is disagreement even within Christianity.
• Many Christians do not believe in purgatory – it is not mentioned by Jesus directly.
• Non-religious people argue there is no scientific evidence for an afterlife.
• People from other religions (e.g. Hindus) believe in reincarnation, not heaven/hell – there is no agreement on what the afterlife looks like.
